rubric.why: Identifies the proportion of gold in 22-carat gold.
rubric.description: States that 22 of the 24 parts are gold.
rubric.how: Award for correctly stating the gold proportion.

rubric.why: Identifies what makes up the remaining parts of the alloy.
rubric.description: States that the remaining 2 parts are other metals, such as copper.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the remaining proportion as other metal(s).

modelAnswer: Gold purity is measured out of 24 parts.
22-carat gold contains 22 parts of gold and 2 parts of other metals, such as copper, in every 24 parts.

items.followUp: State five important points of Rutherford’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Identifies the arrangement of electrons around the nucleus.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed orbits.
rubric.how: Award for the electron-orbit arrangement.

rubric.why: Recognises that each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
rubric.description: States that every orbit has a fixed, definite energy.
rubric.how: Award for the fixed energy of the orbits.

rubric.why: Describes the stability of electrons in permitted orbits.
rubric.description: States that electrons do not radiate energy while in an allowed orbit.
rubric.how: Award for no energy loss in an allowed orbit.

rubric.why: Describes how electrons move to a higher energy level.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs energy to jump to a higher orbit.
rubric.how: Award for the absorption-and-upward-transition point.

rubric.why: Describes how electrons move to a lower energy level.
rubric.description: States that an electron emits energy when it falls to a lower orbit.
rubric.how: Award for the emission-and-downward-transition point.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed circular orbits, also called shells.
Each orbit has a definite, fixed energy.
An electron does not radiate energy while it remains in an allowed orbit.
An electron absorbs energy to jump from a lower orbit to a higher orbit.
An electron emits energy when it falls from a higher orbit to a lower orbit.

items.followUp: A sample contains 1.204×10²⁴ CO₂ molecules. Calculate the amount in moles and its mass.

rubric.why: Uses the correct relationship between number of molecules and moles.
rubric.description: Writes the formula for calculating moles from the number of molecules.
rubric.how: Award for a correct mole formula.

rubric.why: The sample contains half of Avogadro’s number of molecules.
rubric.description: Calculates the amount of CO₂ as 0.50 mol.
rubric.how: Award for the correct amount in moles.

rubric.why: Uses the correct molar mass and mass relationship.
rubric.description: Uses m = nM with the molar mass of CO₂.
rubric.how: Award for the correct mass formula and molar mass.

rubric.why: The product of the amount and molar mass gives the sample’s mass.
rubric.description: Calculates the mass as 0.022 kg (22 g).
rubric.how: Award for the correct mass with a unit.

modelAnswer: Given: number of CO₂ molecules, N = 3.01×10²³; Avogadro constant, Nₐ = 6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹.
Molar mass of CO₂, M = 12 + 2(16) = 44 g mol⁻¹ = 0.044 kg mol⁻¹.
Formula: n = N/Nₐ.
Substitution: n = (3.01×10²³ molecules)/(6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹) = 0.50 mol.
Formula: m = nM.
Substitution: m = (0.50 mol)(0.044 kg mol⁻¹) = 0.022 kg = 22 g.
Answer: The sample contains 0.50 mol of CO₂ and has a mass of 0.022 kg (22 g).

items.followUp: Define hydrogen bonding and describe two effects it has on the properties of water.

rubric.why: A correct definition identifies hydrogen bonding as an attractive intermolecular force.
rubric.description: Defines hydrogen bonding as an attraction involving hydrogen and a highly electronegative atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as an attraction/intermolecular force and 1 mark for specifying the relevant atoms.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding occurs when hydrogen is bonded to a highly electronegative atom, typically F, O, or N, and is attracted to another such atom.
rubric.description: Explains that hydrogen attached to F, O, or N is attracted to a lone pair on a neighbouring molecule.
rubric.how: Award for the explanation with an appropriate atom or example.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonds require additional energy to overcome.
rubric.description: States that hydrogen bonding raises boiling points.
rubric.how: Award for a correct effect on boiling point.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding produces distinctive physical properties.
rubric.description: Gives another valid effect, such as water’s high surface tension or the lower density of ice than liquid water.
rubric.how: Award for one additional correct effect.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom (usually F, O, or N) and a lone pair on an electronegative atom in a neighbouring molecule.
For example, hydrogen bonds form between water molecules.
Hydrogen bonding makes the boiling points of substances higher because extra energy is needed to separate their molecules.
It also gives water a high surface tension; hydrogen bonding makes ice less dense than liquid water.

items.followUp: Define boiling point and explain how external pressure and intermolecular forces affect it.

rubric.why: Boiling occurs when a liquid’s vapour pressure matches the external pressure.
rubric.description: Defines boiling point as the temperature at which vapour pressure equals atmospheric pressure.
rubric.how: Award for the equality of vapour and external/atmospheric pressure.

rubric.why: A higher external pressure requires a higher temperature for the liquid’s vapour pressure to match it.
rubric.description: States that increasing external pressure raises the boiling point.
rubric.how: Award for the correct pressure relationship.

rubric.why: Stronger attractions need more energy to overcome during boiling.
rubric.description: Explains that stronger intermolecular forces raise the boiling point.
rubric.how: Award for the correct intermolecular-force relationship.

rubric.why: Other valid factors include impurities and external pressure.
rubric.description: Gives one further correct factor and its effect, such as non-volatile impurities raising the boiling point.
rubric.how: Award for one additional correctly explained factor.

modelAnswer: The boiling point is the temperature at which the vapour pressure of a liquid becomes equal to the external atmospheric pressure.
Increasing external pressure raises the boiling point; lowering the pressure lowers it.
Stronger intermolecular forces raise the boiling point because more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
Non-volatile impurities generally raise the boiling point of a liquid.

rubric.why: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture.
rubric.description: States that a suspension is heterogeneous.
rubric.how: Award for identifying its heterogeneous nature.

rubric.why: Suspended particles are relatively large and may be seen.
rubric.description: States that suspension particles are large or visible.
rubric.how: Award for a correct statement about particle size or visibility.

rubric.why: Suspension particles settle out when the mixture is left standing.
rubric.description: States that particles settle on standing.
rubric.how: Award for the settling characteristic.

rubric.why: Suspension particles can be removed by filtration.
rubric.description: States that the particles can be separated by filtration.
rubric.how: Award for the filtration characteristic.

modelAnswer: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture.
Its particles are large enough to be visible to the naked eye.
The particles settle down when the suspension is left standing.
The suspended particles can be separated by filtration.

rubric.why: Biochemistry is the branch of chemistry concerned with the chemistry of living organisms.
rubric.description: Defines biochemistry as the study of the chemical substances and processes in living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as a branch/study of chemistry and 1 mark for specifying living organisms or their chemical processes.

modelAnswer: Biochemistry is the branch of chemistry that studies the chemical substances and chemical processes in living organisms.

items.followUp: Define isotope and give one example.

rubric.why: Atomic number is determined by the number of protons in the nucleus.
rubric.description: Defines atomic number as the number of protons in an atom’s nucleus.
rubric.how: Award for the correct definition of atomic number.

rubric.why: The mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
rubric.description: Defines mass number as the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award for the correct definition of mass number.

modelAnswer: Atomic number (Z) is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
Mass number (A) is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
